overview:
On the eighth day Aaron serves at the altar for the first time. Moses tells him to offer a calf and a ram for himself, and the people to bring their own offerings, “for to day the LORD will appear unto you” (v. 4). Aaron offers his own sin offering and burnt offering, his sons bringing him the blood, and then the people’s offerings. He lifts his hand toward the people and blesses them. Moses and Aaron go into the tent, come out, and bless the people again. Fire comes out from before the LORD and consumes the offering on the altar, and the people shout and fall on their faces.

The order matters. Every offering is complete by v. 21, but the LORD’s answer comes only after the blessing and the entry into the tent. The fire does not light a cold altar; it falls on offerings already burning there (vv. 13, 17).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars assign Leviticus to a priestly writer or school.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses’ lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The day after the seven days of ordination (8:33). Jewish tradition makes it the day the tabernacle was raised (Exodus 40:17). Traditional Exodus date about 1446 BC; many scholars prefer the 13th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The court of the tabernacle, before the altar, with the elders and the whole congregation present (vv. 1, 5).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Fire from the LORD consumes offerings again at Solomon’s dedication of the temple (2 Chronicles 7:1) and on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:38).

hermeneutics:
Mesopotamian texts describe the gods as clothed in an overwhelming radiance, Akkadian *melammu*, often paired with *puluhtu*, fear. Temples could be said to wear it, and a god could grant it to a king as a mark of his rule (A. Leo Oppenheim, 1943; Shawn Zelig Aster, 2012). Israel’s word for the visible splendour of God is *kavod*, “glory,” and Leviticus 9 builds toward its appearing. The people’s response matches the old pairing of radiance and dread: they shout and fall on their faces (v. 24). The difference is where the glory shows itself. It rests on no statue in a shrine; it appears “unto all the people” (v. 23) over an altar where a sin offering has just been made for them.

Blessing and prayer went with a raised hand. Babylonian scribes even named a class of prayers after the gesture: the *šu-ila*, “lifting of the hand.” Aaron “lifted up his hand toward the people, and blessed them” (v. 22), turning a gesture usually aimed at a god toward the congregation. Leviticus does not give his words, but Numbers 6:22–27 assigns a fixed blessing to Aaron and his sons, and that blessing is old. Two small silver scrolls found in a tomb at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem, dated to the late 7th or early 6th century BC, carry a text very close to Numbers 6:24–26. They were rolled up and probably worn as amulets, a sign of how much the priestly blessing was valued by ordinary people.

structure.summary: Inclusio: the promise that the LORD will appear (vv. 4, 6) is fulfilled when his glory appears (v. 23).

open.text: “To day the LORD will appear unto you”

close.text: The glory of the LORD appears; fire consumes the offering

notes: **Appear and see:** the Hebrew verb *ra’ah* occurs four times. The LORD “will appear” (vv. 4, 6), his glory “appeared” (v. 23), and the people “saw” the fire (v. 24). *Kavod*, “glory,” occurs only in vv. 6 and 23.
**Commanded:** the verb occurs five times (vv. 5, 6, 7, 10, 21). In v. 21 the subject is Moses: Aaron waves the portions “as Moses commanded.”
**Priest first:** Aaron’s offerings come before the people’s, in the same order, sin offering then burnt offering (vv. 8–14, 15–16).

Ch. 9 closes the ordination unit (8:1–9:24). The seven days at the door end with the eighth day, and the fire from before the LORD answers everything done since 8:1. The opening words of 9:24 return in 10:2, where the same fire kills Nadab and Abihu.
**Backward:** Exodus 40:34–35 ends with the glory filling the tabernacle so that Moses cannot go in. Here Moses and Aaron go in together, and the glory appears to all the people.

traditions.text: Conferring the Priesthood of Aaron on Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery, John the Baptist said it would never be taken from the earth until the sons of Levi “offer again an offering unto the Lord in righteousness.” The words echo Malachi 3:3, where the refiner purifies the sons of Levi so that they may offer in righteousness. Leviticus 9 is the first time the sons of Levi in Aaron’s line offer at all.

In an essay on priesthood read at a conference in Nauvoo, Joseph Smith quoted Malachi 3 and taught that sacrifice was not done away. The offering of sacrifice, he wrote, “forms a part of the duties of the priesthood” and has always been connected with it, and these ordinances will be continued when the priesthood is restored. He tied this to Elijah, who held the keys to administer all its ordinances.
traditions.cite: Instruction on Priesthood, c. 5 Oct. 1840, pp. 8–9 (Joseph Smith Papers)

traditions.text: At the dedication of the Kirtland Temple, Joseph Smith prayed that the Lord’s glory would rest on his people and on the house they dedicated. A week later he and Oliver Cowdery saw the Lord in the temple, who declared, “I have accepted this house.” Leviticus 9 ends the same way, with a sanctuary completed, a blessing given, and the LORD’s glory appearing as a sign of acceptance.

Speaking from the darkness after his death, the Lord tells the Nephites that their sacrifices and burnt offerings are done away and that he will accept none of them. In their place they are to offer a broken heart and a contrite spirit, and he will baptize such people “with fire and with the Holy Ghost.” The fire that once fell on the altar is now promised to the offerer.

A baraita says the day the tabernacle was raised “took ten crowns.” It was the first day of creation’s week, the first day of the princes’ offerings, the first of the priesthood, the first of service, the first descent of fire, the first eating of holy food, the first resting of the Divine Presence, the first priestly blessing of Israel, the first day private altars were forbidden, and the first of the months. Rashi identifies that day with the eighth day of this chapter.

Why did Moses and Aaron go into the tent (v. 23)? One answer is that Moses taught Aaron the incense service. Another is that when every offering was done and no fire had come, Aaron was ashamed and said the LORD must be angry with him; Moses went in with him, they prayed, and the Divine Presence came down. Moses had told the people that through Aaron’s service they would know their sin with the golden calf was forgiven.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Lev 9:23; Sifra, Mekhilta deMiluim 2:18

traditions.text: Philo says that on the eighth day Moses led his brother into the tabernacle and taught him, like a teacher with a pupil, how the high priest should minister within. When they came out and raised their hands in prayer for the nation, a body of flame burst from the inmost shrine and fell on the altar. Whether it was pure ether or air turned to fire, he says, it showed that nothing done there happened without God’s providence.

Josephus says that on the eighth day Moses made a feast for the people, who competed with one another in the sacrifices they brought. As the sacrifices lay on the altar, a fire kindled from among them “of its own accord,” looking like a flash of lightning, and consumed everything on the altar. Philo has the fire come from the shrine; Josephus has it rise from the offerings.

The letter in 2 Maccabees sets this scene beside the temple’s dedication: as when Moses prayed, the fire came down from heaven and consumed the sacrifices, so Solomon prayed and fire came down. The next line remembers Moses saying that the sin offering was consumed because it was not to be eaten, a memory of the dispute in 10:16–20.

Hebrews says every high priest taken from among men must offer for sins “as for the people, so also for himself,” because he too is beset with weakness. That is the order of vv. 7–15, where Aaron’s calf comes before the people’s goat. Hebrews then sets Christ apart as a high priest who has no need to offer first for his own sins.
